subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: At the school water fountain Abhinav slipped and fell hard, and his tiffin skidded across the floor. About twenty children were in the corridor. Jaya stood with her water bottle, watching. Everyone else was watching too, and a few whispered. Somebody will go, Jaya thought. Somebody will tell Ma'am. Abhinav sat holding his knee. Nobody moved. A bell rang, and the crowd drifted off in twos and threes. Jaya walked to class with a tight throat, wondering how many of the others had thought exactly the same thing.

qa.q: About how many children were in the corridor when Abhinav fell?
qa.a: About twenty children were in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking while standing with the water bottle?
qa.a: Jaya assumed somebody else would go and tell Ma'am, so the sense of duty felt spread among everyone; afterwards the tight throat shows guilt and unease.

qa.q: What could Jaya do at that moment instead of waiting?
qa.a: Jaya could point at one person, or walk to the nearest teacher and say "Abhinav fell and needs help", since one clear step ends the waiting.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have experienced twenty children watching and nobody coming?
qa.a: Abhinav may have felt embarrassed and alone, holding a hurt knee while everyone watched but no one came near.

grounding: A child sees another child fall and does nothing because many others are watching too, each assuming someone else will step in.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: From the school bus window I saw it. Vandana fell off the swing and sat holding her elbow. About ten children formed a ring around her. Anirban was in it, twisting a shirt button. He looked at the girl next to him, who looked at the boy next to her. Everyone seemed to be waiting for somebody. After a full minute a girl at the back ran off toward the staff room, and the ring melted. I do not know what Anirban was thinking, but he was the last to leave, still looking back at Vandana.

qa.q: What was Anirban doing while standing in the ring?
qa.a: Anirban was twisting a shirt button.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been feeling while looking at the girl next to him?
qa.a: Anirban may have been uneasy and unsure, waiting for someone else to move first; looking back at Vandana suggests some guilt, though the narrator cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Anirban have done in that first minute?
qa.a: Anirban could have pointed to one person and said "You, get Ma'am", or gone to the staff room himself, which breaks the waiting.

qa.q: What might Vandana have experienced during the minute when the ring of children stayed still?
qa.a: Vandana probably felt hurt, embarrassed and alone, sitting with a sore elbow while ten children watched without acting.

grounding: A child sees another child fall and waits for others to act, and a bystander's account shows each assuming someone else will step in.
